extracted.intended_audience: students and readers interested in public opinion, journalism, and communication (journalists, political scientists, policymakers)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and observations for how news and ideas are produced, transmitted, and consumed in a society — including channels of distribution, barriers to access, attention limits, linguistic problems, and social gating. Useful for evaluating journalism, propaganda campaigns, and public-information strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and comprehensiveness of distribution machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: The effectiveness of a campaign or news effort depends on assembling extensive machinery — e.g., divisions issuing thousands of releases, tens of thousands of speakers, posters, lantern slides, periodicals, and using civic and religious organizations as channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: Creel's World War I effort with a Division of News issuing more than six thousand releases, seventy-five thousand Four Minute Men delivering 755,190 speeches, thousands of posters and other materials. Assess whether the program uses multiple channels (speakers, print, organizations) and the numerical scale necessary to reach 'one public opinion.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusiveness of channels in peacetime vs crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: In wartime extraordinary measures can create a near-uniform public opinion; in peacetime similar inclusive reach rarely exists, leaving large sections, enclaves and classes that hear only vaguely about much that is going on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether communication efforts reach marginalized or isolated groups outside dominant channels; note that absence of crisis-level mobilization tends to leave ghettoes and enclaves underinformed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infrastructure effects on circulation of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Transport and communications infrastructure (railways, ports, cables, highways, mail, radio, shipping lines, aeroplanes) affect both the supply and quality of information and opinion in intricate ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how changes in infrastructure (new railways/ports, censorship/uncensoring of cables, changes in mail speed, tariffs) alter access and flow of news; examples include a city declining when shipbuilding changes redirect international influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly, cost, and supply as barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Monopolizing of cables, ports, canals, terminals, etc., is a barrier to exchange of news and opinion, but cost and limited supply can be even greater barriers than monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess economic and structural obstacles (tariffs, subsidies, scarcity of facilities) that prevent equitable circulation of information; monopoly is not the only or necessarily the largest obstacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Income as determinant of access
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of a man's income has considerable effect on his access to the world beyond his neighborhood — with money one can travel, buy books and periodicals, and overcome tangible obstacles to communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating information reach, account for socio-economic differences: wealthier individuals/communities can secure more communication and broader exposure; also consider how ideas influence spending choices and long-term income.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-imposed limitations of curiosity and engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Some people, though not constrained by external barriers, 'suffer from anemia, from lack of appetite and curiosity for the human scene' and thus do not access available information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between structural lack of access and voluntary disengagement; strategies to inform must consider motivation and interests as well as availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social set as gatekeeper of admissible information
rubrics_metrics.description: The social set determines which authorities and sources of information are admissible and shapes judgments by the canons of Family Tradition, Respectability, Propriety, Dignity, Taste and Form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how tightly knit social groups filter and sanction information (who 'figures as people in the phrase

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of social leaders and inter-set channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Social leaders and exceptional people who move in and out of sets create personal channels across sets, through which imitation and circulation of standards occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether opinion leaders bridge social sets; presence of such connectors increases diffusion of ideas beyond narrow circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of public affairs in elite social sets
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Highest Society the big decisions of war and peace, and ultimate distribution of political power, are intimate experiences within a circle of personal acquaintances — the private affairs of this set are public matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing influence, consider how elite social circles conflate private and public spheres and thus disproportionately shape national and foreign policy discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited time and attention for news
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals typically spend a small amount of time each day directly exposed to information about public affairs — survey estimates cluster around a quarter of an hour a day for many groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical estimates (Hotchkiss & Franken; Scott) showing most respondents report ~15 minutes/day; design and evaluate news content for very limited daily attention budgets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of reader interest across newspaper features
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers' stated interests (general news, editorials, politics, finance, foreign news, local news) and newspaper space allocation (news, opinion, literature, illustrations, advertisements) show a relationship between demand and supply of topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference figures from Wilcox and surveys: after excluding ads, about 76.5% of space (1900) dealt with public-affairs topics; compare reader preferences (e.g., 67% interested in public affairs) with editorial allocation when evaluating editorial strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of brevity and telescoping of meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A few words must often stand for a whole succession of acts, thoughts, feelings and consequences; journalists must telescope meaning so readers can judge how much weight to give to a news item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing or evaluating brief news items, check whether the condensed language preserves cues allowing readers to assess reliability and significance; recognize impossibility of full justice in terse accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding, translation, and transmission compromise fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: Press service news is usually coded for telegraphy; long speeches in foreign tongues are translated, coded, decoded and transcribed by operators — each step can distort or lose nuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how coding (Phillip's Code example), translation and operator transcription may alter substance; factor in transmission processes when judging accuracy and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words are imperfect and culturally variable in meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Words evoke different images in different readers; national tendencies to understate or overstate lead to 'inflation' or 'deflation' in word-value; identical terms may carry different weight across languages and cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cross-cultural and lexical differences; consider 'word exchanges' where equivalents carry different connotations (example: translating 'distinguished scholar' into French), and adjust interpretation of foreign press accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience heterogeneity in literacy and comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Millions can hardly read; millions can read but not understand; of those who do understand, only a minority have time to devote attention — thus the public is highly heterogeneous in ability to process news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and evaluate information with multiple audience strata in mind (illiterate, low comprehension, limited time); ensure key cues are accessible to less informed readers while allowing depth for more attentive ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lucidity: ability to dissociate superficial analogies and attend to differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Lucidity of mind is the faculty to dissociate superficial analogies, attend to differences and appreciate variety; it is essential for constructing sound public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging arguments or reporting, prioritize clarity that helps readers distinguish crude perceptions and vague analogies; promote critical thinking rather than reflexive imitation.
